claims.text: The target material is a phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy.
A dopant having strong affinity for phosphorus should replace 1–5 at% of the original alloy composition.
Adding 1–5 at% of a phosphorus-affine dopant will reduce the alloy's liquidus temperature.
Adding the dopant will suppress crystallization pathways.
Doping will increase the glass-transition temperature relative to an undoped reference.
Doping will increase the onset temperature of crystallization relative to an undoped reference.
Arc melting at approximately 1700–1800 K under inert atmosphere is an appropriate fabrication condition for the proposed alloys.
Rapid quenching at at least 10^4 K/s favors formation of the amorphous state.
Dopant–phosphorus interactions locally disrupt crystallization sites.
Dopant–phosphorus interactions increase chemical short-range disorder and thereby stabilize the supercooled liquid.
Strong dopant–phosphorus bonding lowers crystal nucleation and growth kinetics.
The reduction in nucleation and growth kinetics is mediated by a lower liquidus temperature and increased local packing frustration.
The doped alloys should exhibit a DSC-measured upward shift of approximately 10–20 K in both Tg and Tx.
Upward shifts in Tg and Tx indicate improved glass-forming ability and greater thermal stability of the amorphous phase.
Dopant additions above approximately 5 at% may produce detrimental intermetallic phases and reduce glass-forming ability.
Low cooling rates can diminish the proposed beneficial effect.
An undoped alloy processed identically provides the direct experimental control.
Failure of both Tg and Tx to increase by approximately 10–20 K, or equal or reduced thermal stability, would falsify the hypothesis.
